One resonant plant, one fixed drive-power budget, and every excitation you might reach for:
**optimal, flat, and shaped multisines** (Schroeder, random, or cophased phase), **linear and
logarithmic swept sines**, and **broadband and shaped noise**. Pick any of them and watch two
numbers — and the whole scoreboard — update live, all in your browser, no install.

## The two axes

Every drive here spends the **same total power**. What changes is *how* it spends it, and that
splits cleanly into two independent stories:

- **Time to identify to 5%** — set by the drive's **power spectrum** $P_{xx}(f)$ alone. This is
  the real Cramér–Rao bound (the same Fisher kernel as the [landing-page game](index.qmd) and the
  [`system_ident` pipeline](examples/interactive.qmd)). Pile power where the plant's modal
  parameters are least certain and the clock plummets; spread it flat and you wait ~40× longer.
  Notice that *every* flat-spectrum drive — flat multisine, white noise, a linear sweep — shares
  the **same** time, whatever its phase. Fisher can't tell them apart.

- **Crest factor at the DAC** — set by the **phases**, not the power. Two drives with an identical
  spectrum can differ 8× in crest: a **Schroeder** multisine flattens the waveform toward the
  $\sqrt2$ single-tone floor, **random** phases give a noise-like ~3.4, and **cophased** lines pile
  into an impulse (~15) that a real actuator would clip. Crest is measured on the actual samples the
  DAC would emit — no whitening-filter sleight of hand.

## Why the optimal multisine wins

Put the two together and the champion (★) is the **Fisher-optimal multisine with Schroeder
phase**: fastest *and* low-crest. A swept sine matches its crest but wastes power off-resonance;
broadband noise is beaten on both axes (and, not shown here, pays a further leakage / variance
penalty for being aperiodic). That is the entire case for
[optimal excitation](tutorial/why-optimal-excitation.qmd) — here it is something you can *feel* by
clicking, before a single equation.
